newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers upbeat as Kohl gives EMU fillip.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers upbeat as Kohl gives EMU fillip.

text.p: EU finance ministers gathered on Friday for a two-day meeting to advance single currency plans in an upbeat mood, cheered by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to seek re-election next year and lead the drive for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Following a welter of speculation about a delay in EMU's planned 1999 start-date, the 15 ministers welcomed Thursday's announcement that Kohl, the key figure behind the single currency, will stand for a fifth term of office.
His decision gave a shot in the arm to the pro-EMU camp, which appears to have been out-shouted in recent weeks by those who doubt the euro project can start on schedule.
Ministers arriving in this Dutch coastal resort said Kohl's decision to stand again sent a clear signal to any doubters.
"...Chancellor Kohl is one of the big European politicians with a very clear vision for the future of Europe," Danish Economics Minister Marianne Jelved told Reuters.
"If anyone had any doubts about EMU starting on time, I can't see any reason for those doubts after this decision."
"This shows that he's very committed to seeing the single currency through," said Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn.
German participation in the first wave of EMU is seen as critical to the venture's success.

But, with German unemployment at its highest since Hitler came to power 64 years ago and Bonn risking worker unrest in a determined bid to cut spending to meet EMU criteria, many have voiced doubts that the single currency can start on time.
Analysts said the markets had picked up on the more pro-EMU news coming out of Germany which, they said, improved the viability of the EMU project.
"There are a couple of things going on in the background which are helping to shore up confidence," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London.

One factor was Kohl's announcement he would run again in 1998. The other was the recent set of unexpectedly strong economic data in Germany, which needs an economic pickup to improve the ratio between its fiscal deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) -- one of the key targets to qualify for EMU.

Ministers, who are expected to reaffirm a commitment to EMU's 1999 launch date, will have welcomed Thursday's recovery in German industrial output which rebounded in February to a 1.9 percent rise after January's 1.5 percent fall.
But they will also discuss the more general European picture of sluggish growth, rising unemployment and efforts by some members to meet the conditions for joining the single currency.
Those wanting to join in EMU, scheduled to start in January 1999, must bring their 1997 budget deficits close to three percent of GDP under the targets set by the Maastricht Treaty.
Ministers will try on Saturday to set a date next year for choosing which states join EMU from the start.

The odds favour late April 1998, allowing France to complete its parliamentary election and giving time to consider key reports, due in February, from the European Commission and the European Monetary Institute on economic convergence within the 15-nation bloc.

Ministers will also review progress on EMU's technical aspects, adding legal context to a stability and growth pact, which seeks to penalise governments running excessive budget deficits -- above three percent of GDP -- inside EMU.
In addition, they will take stock of negotiations on a revamped Exchange Rate Mechanism designed to link countries outside EMU to the euro.
Jelved said she expected a positive session. "I don't expect dramatic or hard discussions, but a very calm and good meeting."
